weeks.objective: Ask precise who, where, and why questions. Short a and final-e a

connection.before: Grade 1 blending, short-vowel and final-e reading, and oral retelling are checked rather than assumed.
connection.after: Next week, apply this evidence work to separate what happened from why it happened; word work moves to short i and final-e i.

days: Day 1: Introduce short a and final-e a. Model tape; blend fresh words with feedback. Adult reads The Bench with Two Jobs; discuss the worked evidence example.
Day 2: Revisit the story for ask precise who, where, and why questions; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read The Safe Box independently after word preparation.
Day 3: Adult reads Our Garden Supply Station; examine the organization and vocabulary in each. Connect its details to the story without treating fiction as factual evidence.
Day 4: Use worksheet B, repair printed-word errors, and reread The Safe Box with meaningful phrases; record accuracy and support, not a speed race.
Day 5: Select worksheet C for transfer. Ask for a new text-supported oral explanation and hear an individual rereading; reteach observed word patterns.
explanation: A question word tells us what sort of answer to look for. Who asks for a person; where asks for a place; why asks for a reason. In this story, merely naming Nell does not answer why she moves the basket. Follow her observation of Grandfather and the crowded seat. A careful answer can join two details even when no sentence starts with because. Recount the change before suggesting a lesson.

The information text has one broad topic, the garden supply station, but each paragraph does a smaller job. Paragraph 2 is about seed storage, not every supply. Use the paragraph number to locate supporting details. A label such as SEEDS helps a reader find a place; the sentence about splashes explains why that place is useful. Do not substitute a personal garden idea for a detail this author actually gives.

A closed syllable such as cap usually has short a; a consonant followed by final e can mark long a as in cape. Model tape: Read tape by blending t | a_e | p. The t and p keep their consonant sounds; a_e spells long a, so blend /t/ + long a + /p/ to say tape. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach the high-frequency words has, his, the, from, and a; explicitly teach ar in far and review sh in the adult directions. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: The Bench with Two Jobs
passages.text:
At the edge of the school garden stood a low wooden bench. Nell put a basket of seed packets on it before the garden club arrived. When Amir came with his grandfather, Grandfather paused beside the path and rubbed his knee. Nell moved one packet to make a tiny space. Grandfather still stood.
Nell looked again. The basket filled almost the entire seat. She carried it to the wide stump beside the watering cans. “The seeds can wait here,” she said. Grandfather sat down and began telling the children how he kept seed packets dry. Nell brought him one packet at a time. By the end of the visit, the bench had held a person and the children had gained a useful idea. Nell was glad she had looked twice.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Our Garden Supply Station
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: A supply station keeps tools and materials in one place. At our class garden, the station has a low shelf, a lidded box, and a hook. Children return each item after using it so the next gardener can find it.
Paragraph 2: Seed packets belong in the lidded box. The lid keeps splashes away from the paper. A damp packet can become hard to read. The label on the box says SEEDS.
Paragraph 3: The watering cans hang from the hook when empty. Wet tools go on the open shelf to dry before they are put away. Each storage place has a different job.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Safe Box
passages.text: Sam has a flat box. The box has a lid. Sam can tape a tag on it. The tag has his name. A wet rag is on the mat. Sam sets the rag far from his safe box.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

connection.before: Build on week 1: Ask precise who, where, and why questions.

days: Day 1: Introduce short i and final-e i. Model pine; blend fresh words with feedback. Adult reads A Bell for the Kitten; discuss the worked evidence example.
Day 2: Revisit the story for separate what happened from why it happened; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read A Fine Hike independently after word preparation.

explanation: What happened names an action; why it happened explains its reason. Pip hides when visitors arrive, but the text does not tell us every thought in her head. Use cautious words such as seems when inferring that she is uneasy. Luis first tries carrying her; later he gives her time. A recount should preserve that change instead of saying only that children played with a kitten.

A whole-text topic should cover all paragraphs without becoming vague. The quiet-corner plan includes making, placing, and keeping an entrance clear. Paragraph 2 is narrower: it explains placement away from a busy door. This is a classroom model with a toy, not instructions for caring for a real animal. Keep the author’s stated purpose and the fictional kitten’s experience distinct.

Contrast short i in closed syllables with long i marked by final e. Model pine: Read pine by blending p | i_e | n. Keep /p/ and /n/ around the i_e spelling; i_e says long i, giving pine rather than pin. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Mike, Kim, wide, path, them, calls, and thanks; explicitly review ay in way, ar in far, and known blends, plus the previous a_e pattern. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: A Bell for the Kitten
passages.text:
Pip the kitten slipped behind the curtain whenever a visitor rang the doorbell. Once the guests had gone, she came out and searched for her red ball. Luis wanted Pip to meet his cousin. He carried the kitten toward the door, but Pip wriggled free and hid again.
The next afternoon, Luis asked his cousin to sit quietly on the rug. He placed the red ball nearby and waited. For a long time only the curtain moved. Then one gray paw reached out. Pip rolled the ball toward the cousin, who rolled it gently back. Luis did not pick Pip up. By the end of the game she was sitting between them. “You came when you were ready,” Luis whispered.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Quiet Corner Plan
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: Our pretend animal-care room has a quiet corner for a visiting toy animal. This classroom design helps us think about space and comfort. We use a cardboard box with a wide opening and a folded cloth inside.
Paragraph 2: We place the corner away from the classroom door. The door is a busy place because people enter, leave, and hang up bags there. A sign reminds classmates to walk softly near the corner.
Paragraph 3: We leave the opening clear. A toy can be moved in and out easily when blocks and bags do not cover the entrance. After play, we check the entrance again.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: Mike can hike on a wide path. A big twig is in his way. Mike lifts it and sets it to the side. Kim can ride past. “Thanks!” Kim calls. Mike grins. The path is wide and safe for them.

passages.title: The Last Blue Square
passages.text:
Mara and Jo were making a paper sea for the library window. Blue squares covered the table, but only one dark blue square remained. “I need it for my whale,” said Mara. “My boat needs a deep wave,” said Jo. They each held a corner until the paper began to wrinkle.
Jo let go first. He laid his boat beside Mara’s unfinished whale. The picture looked strange with the boat floating in empty white space. Mara set the dark square between the two shapes. “What if it belongs to the sea?” she asked. They cut a wide strip for the water and used the leftover corners for the whale’s tail and the boat’s shadow. At the window, both children pointed to the same dark wave. Neither called it mine.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Planning a Paper Picture
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: A paper picture can be planned before anything is glued down. Place the largest shapes on the background first. Move them until there is room for the other parts. This loose arrangement is called a layout.
Paragraph 2: Save useful scraps in a tray. A long strip can become a path; a triangle can become a roof. Keeping scraps together makes them easier to find when a small shape is needed.
Paragraph 3: Glue only after checking the whole picture. A shape that works alone may cover an important part of its neighbor. Looking at the whole layout helps the maker notice that problem.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Note at Home
passages.text: Rose left a note on a box at home. “Do not toss this box,” it said. “It has rocks in it.” Tom read the note. He set the box on a low shelf. Rose came back and smiled at the safe rocks.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

explanation: When questions locate an event in time; how questions ask about a process or change. A good recount tracks Tessa’s shift from disappointment to close observation. Do not erase her original wish: she still wants to see the bridge. A character can gain a new interest without abandoning an old one. The ending’s wish to walk slowly shows the effect of the small discoveries.

The information text separates an observation walk into preparation, work at a stop, and discussion afterward. The whole topic is not simply pencils or colors. Each paragraph’s narrower focus answers a different question about the activity. Distinguish a detail in the text from an example a student might add: an invented observation may be sensible but is not evidence for what the class actually did.

Compare short u with u_e, which can say /yoo/ in cube or /oo/ in flute. Model cube: Read cube by blending c | u_e | b. The c says /k/ and b says /b/; u_e says long u, /yoo/, in cube. Preteach June, she, puts, float, eats, her, and of; accept dialect variation in long-u pronunciation. passages.title: When the Path Was Closed
passages.text:
On Saturday, Tessa took a sketchbook to the park pond. She wanted to draw the little wooden bridge. A sign across the path read CLOSED FOR REPAIR. Tessa sighed and sat on a stone. “Now there is nothing to draw,” she said. Her brother Ben pointed to a snail beside her shoe.
Tessa bent low. The snail’s shell had a curling line, and its soft body stretched far beyond the shell. She drew the curl first. Then she noticed a bent reed reflected in a puddle and a tiny feather caught in the grass. Her page slowly filled. On the walk home, Ben asked if she still wanted to see the bridge. “Yes,” she said, “but I want to walk slowly on the way.”
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Close-Looking Walk
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: In our class close-looking walk, partners stop at three marked places in the school yard. The goal is to describe what is present rather than collect it. Each pair carries a clipboard and pencil.
Paragraph 2: At a stop, one partner names a detail while the other draws or writes it. They can describe shape, color, position, or movement. Then the partners trade jobs.
Paragraph 3: Back in class, pairs compare their records. Two pairs may have noticed different details at the same place. The class adds these observations to one shared page without deciding that only one pair looked correctly.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

explanation: A fable can use talking animals to explore a human habit. Rabbit’s proud talk matters because it connects his empty basket to his choices, not merely to bad luck. A lesson should travel beyond the exact berries: paying attention to useful work matters more than showing off equipment. Accept another lesson only when the reader links it to real events, such as Mole’s practical choices or generosity.

The information text explains sorting classroom models. The topic stays the same across paragraphs while the focus moves from choosing a feature, to keeping a rule, to checking the result. A reader should not mix story-world berry picking with factual advice about edible fruit. The counters are explicitly not food; their color is a sorting feature, not a sign that something is safe to eat.

Short e occurs in many closed syllables; compare it with familiar long vowels without assuming every final e has the same role. Model step: Read step by blending s | t | e | p. Say the /s/ and /t/ separately in the blend, use short e, and finish with /p/: step. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach toy, was, for, said, this, and the name Pete; review blends in scraps and step. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: Rabbit’s Empty Basket
passages.text:
Rabbit polished his basket and hurried to the berry patch. Mole had arrived first and was reaching for a low branch. “Your basket is too small,” Rabbit said. “Mine will carry twice as much.” He raced past Mole toward the tallest bush.
All morning Rabbit searched for berries that would look grand in his grand basket. He passed small ripe berries and stretched for large green ones that were not ready. Mole filled her little basket with the ripe berries within reach. When a soft rain began, Mole headed home. Rabbit looked inside his shining basket. It held one leaf. Mole offered him half her snack beneath a broad branch. Rabbit thanked her and began looking at the berries instead of the basket.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Sorting the Classroom Collection
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: Our class sorts a collection of wooden counters shaped like fruit. The counters are models, not food. Sorting means putting objects into groups using a chosen feature. We can group by color, shape, or size.
Paragraph 2: A sorting rule must stay the same while the group is being made. If the rule is color, a small red counter and a large red counter belong together. Size does not change their color.
Paragraph 3: After sorting, we explain the rule and check every group. A counter in the wrong group can be moved. We can then start again with a different rule and get different groups from the same collection.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: Ben set a red box on a step. It was a nest box for a toy hen. He put soft scraps in it. The toy hen fit well. “This is the best spot,” Ben said. He left the box on the step.

passages.title: The Name on the Card
passages.text:
At the class sharing table, Eden found a card that read FOR THE NEW READER. Beside it stood a tiny book with a cloth cover. Eden had read her first long story that week. She reached for the book. Across the table, Sami reached too. He had just learned to read a sign on his own.
Neither child moved the gift. Instead, they took the card to Ms. Lane. She laughed softly. “I forgot the most useful word,” she said. She wrote EVERY on a fresh card: FOR EVERY NEW READER. The tiny book held blank pages. Each child could add the name of something newly read. Eden wrote her story title, and Sami drew his sign and copied its words. The book stayed at the sharing table, growing one small success at a time.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Record with a Purpose
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: Our reading record collects examples of new reading. An entry includes the reader’s chosen name, the date, and a title or short description. A record helps a class notice growth over time.
Paragraph 2: A useful entry is specific. “I read something” tells little. “I read the bus-stop sign” names the reading clearly. A drawing can be added when a description is difficult to write.
Paragraph 3: The class reviews the record at the end of the month. Readers can notice different kinds of reading, including stories, labels, poems, and directions. The record is not a race to fill the most lines.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: Jake and Meg plan a game. A stone is the goal. Meg can hop to it. Jake can slide a flat disk to it. They take turns. No one wins each time. “A game is fun for both of us,” says Meg.

passages.title: The Bent Invitation
passages.text:
Asha made an invitation shaped like a rainbow. On the way to deliver it, rain spotted the paper. She pressed it flat beneath her coat, but one corner bent. At Leo’s door, Asha nearly hid the card. “It was better before,” she said. Leo read the invitation slowly. “A puppet show! What time?” Asha pointed to the blurred numbers and frowned.
They went inside and copied the time onto a dry strip. Asha pasted the strip across the bent corner like a tiny banner. Leo put the card where his family could see it. Asha’s rainbow was crooked, but its message was clear.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Make a Standing Card
passages.text:
Materials: One sheet of paper and a pencil.
Fold: Bring the two short edges together. Press the fold. Open the paper partway so it stands like a small tent.
Write: Put the open side down. Write a name on the outside face that you can see.
Check: Set the card on a table and read it from across the table. If the writing is upside down, turn the paper before making a new card. The check comes last because a flat sheet does not show how the finished card will stand.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Bridge for Three
passages.text:
Noor set two toy sheep on a paper bridge. The bridge sagged, but it held. “There is room for one more,” said Eli, setting down a third sheep. The middle sank onto the table. Noor swept the sheep away. “We need stronger paper!” she said.
Eli folded the same sheet into a zigzag and placed it across the blocks again. Noor watched, unsure. They tested one sheep, then two, then three. The folded paper stayed above the table. Noor drew a zigzag beside her first flat bridge sketch. Under both pictures she wrote, “Same paper, different shape.” Now the failed bridge was part of their record instead of something to hide.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Test a Paper Bridge
passages.text:
Set Up: Place two equal blocks one hand-width apart on a table. Lay a sheet of paper across them. Use three matching counters as the load.
First Test: Add counters one at a time. Record whether the paper still spans the gap after each counter.
Change: Fold the same sheet into a zigzag. Keep the blocks and gap unchanged.
Second Test: Add the same counters one at a time again. Compare the records. Keeping the gap and load alike helps you examine the effect of the paper’s shape. A different paper or gap would change more than one feature.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

Day 2: Revisit the story for use a story’s beginning to explain its ending; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read The Slow Boat independently after word preparation.

explanation: The beginning supplies information needed to understand the ending. Finn blows from far away, then succeeds after changing his position. The cousin’s visit lets him apply what he learned. A reader should not infer that the boat changed: the red mark establishes that the same boat was present. Track the evidence that corrects Finn’s first explanation.

A short contents guide maps topics to paragraph numbers. Use it to locate instructions efficiently, then read the paragraph rather than trusting the heading alone. The procedure separates observed results from measurements: saying a boat moved is different from claiming an exact distance. Neither the story nor the procedure supplies a distance to calculate.

Oa and ow can represent long o; teach ow in snow and grow here, while reserving its other sound for later contrast. Model float: Read float by blending f | l | oa | t. Blend /f/ and /l/, long o for oa, and /t/; float has one vowel sound and one syllable. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach warm, room, window, edge, drifts, Mo, and Jo; review ai and ee before adding long-o teams. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: The Boat That Would Not Go
passages.text:
Finn’s toy boat sat still in a shallow pan. He puffed from one end of the table, but the boat did not move. His sister Mira put her face near the pan and blew softly. The boat glided to the far edge. Finn folded his arms. “You have a better boat,” he said.
Mira pointed to the little red mark Finn had drawn on its side. It was his boat. She moved his chair closer to the pan. This time his breath reached the sail. The boat crossed the water, and Finn laughed. When his cousin arrived, Finn moved a chair close for her too. He did not promise a magic boat. He showed her where to sit.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Arrange a Fair Toy-Boat Try
passages.text:
Find It Fast: Setup—paragraph 1; Taking Turns—paragraph 2; Notes—paragraph 3.
Paragraph 1: Place a shallow pan on a stable table. An adult adds a small amount of water and places a toy sailboat in it. Mark one chair position close to the pan.
Paragraph 2: Each child uses that chair and starts the boat at the same edge. Another person resets the boat between turns. This keeps the starting arrangement alike.
Paragraph 3: Record what happened before changing the arrangement. Notes might say that the boat moved or stayed still. Do not write a distance unless it was actually measured.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: A toy boat floats in a pan. Snow is at the window, but the room is warm. Mo blows on the boat. It goes from side to side. “Go slow,” says Jo. Mo stops, and the boat drifts to the edge.

Preteach moth, flies, ties, kite, latch, helps, and day; teach ie in pie and tie explicitly before the fresh sentence. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. passages.title: The Lantern Line
passages.text:
Ivo wanted every paper lantern in a straight line. He placed the first four on the shelf, then frowned at the fifth. Its handle leaned sideways. He tried squeezing it straight, but the paper creased. “This one ruins the line,” he said.
Mae set a small wooden block under the leaning lantern. Its light-shaped paper window now stood higher than the others. She raised two more lanterns with blocks of different heights. Ivo stepped back. The row looked like a little town climbing a hill. He stopped squeezing the handle and moved the tallest lantern to the end. For the class display, he wrote a new label: A Town of Lanterns. None of the paper lanterns held a real flame.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Paper Lantern Display
passages.text:
Contents: 1—Prepare the shelf; 2—Arrange; 3—Label.
1. Prepare the shelf. Clear a steady shelf and lay down a paper mat. Use only paper models; do not add flame or heat.
2. Arrange. Place sturdy blocks on the mat before placing paper lanterns on the blocks. Check that each model stays upright. Move unstable models to the mat.
3. Label. Write a label after the arrangement is settled. The label should describe what viewers will actually see. A title chosen too early may no longer match the display.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: At night, a bright light is on by the gate. A moth flies by it. Dad ties a tag to a kite. “We will fly it in the day,” he says. The kite stays inside. The light helps Dad see the latch.

passages.title: The Book Nook Sign
passages.text:
Lena painted BOOK NOOK in huge blue letters. She held the sign above the classroom shelf and smiled. Then Ben stood across the room. “I can read BOOK,” he said, “but your plant is hiding the other word.” Lena tugged the sign higher. Now it covered the clock.
She set the sign on the table and made two smaller cards. One said BOOK; the other said NOOK. She placed them side by side on the front of the shelf, below the plant and the clock. Ben walked back to the far wall and read both words. Lena kept the huge sign on the work table as a reminder: a sign’s job is to be seen, not just to look bold up close.

passages.title: Find a Place for a Sign
passages.text:
Heading: Choose. Pick the place that the sign names. A sign for a shelf should be close enough that readers can connect the words with the shelf.
Heading: Test. Hold the sign in place. Ask a partner to look from the usual reading spot. Check whether a plant, door, or other object hides any letters.
Heading: Fix. Move the sign or change its size if necessary, then test again. A large sign is not always the easiest to read if part of it is blocked.
Glossary: blocked—hidden from view by something in the way.

passages.title: Cloud Shapes, Clear Steps
passages.text:
Arlo’s class was making a cloud mural. Arlo wanted one enormous cloud, so he brushed paint across a whole sheet. The wet paper sagged when he lifted it. He put it down and stared at the puddle around its edge. “I cannot hang this,” he said.
Zuri slid a dry board beneath the sheet. They left it flat while they made labels for the mural. Later the paint was dry and the paper could be lifted. Arlo used both hands and carried it on the board to the wall. He told the next painter, “The cloud can be big, but it needs time and support.” The mural grew slowly, with space on the table for one drying sheet at a time.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Dry a Classroom Painting
passages.text:
Quick Guide: Drying place—A; Moving the work—B; Starting the next painting—C.
A. Put the wet painting on a flat board or protected table. Leave it there until the paint is dry. Wet paper can bend easily.
B. Ask an adult to help move a large painting. Keep a board beneath it while carrying it. Remove the board only when the paper has another steady support.
C. Clear the drying place before beginning another large sheet. A free space prevents a new painting from being stacked on wet work.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Tap, Tap, Stop
passages.text:
Tap, tap, tap on the tabletop,
Pat the rhythm, then we stop.
Soft as slippers down the hall,
Loud as blocks that tumble, fall.
Tap, tap, tap, then wait and hear:
Even silence has a place here.

“I want the loud part,” said Bea, lifting two wooden spoons. “It wakes the room.”
“I like the space after it,” said Dev. “Then I can hear the last tap fade.”
They tried the poem together. Bea made the big sounds, and Dev held up a hand for the pauses. When Bea nearly tapped through the final quiet, she saw his hand and waited. The room seemed to hold its breath.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Rhythm Score
passages.text:
This guide explains a classroom rhythm score. A score is a written plan for sounds. In our score, X means one tap, and a dash means one silent beat. Each symbol takes the same amount of time.
Pattern: X X X —. Read it as tap, tap, tap, rest. Repeat the four beats without making the rest shorter. Silence is part of this pattern, not a place to hurry.
Partners can take different jobs. One makes the taps while the other points to each symbol. Then they exchange jobs so both practice sound and silence.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

explanation: Two characters can see the same setting and interpret it differently. Miri sees a lost outing; Sol sees an opportunity to draw. Neither view changes the fact that rain is falling. Her final action shows a partial change, not a total reversal: she keeps the drawing but still wants the park. Preserve that mixed response when describing her perspective.

The author describes an observation page and explains the jobs of its sections. Observation and feeling are not competing claims; they answer different questions. The supplied examples make that distinction concrete. A record can include both if the writer labels them clearly. Do not classify disappointment as a false observation; it is a real response recorded in a different place.

In a two-syllable word, inspect each part; a final-e syllable may keep a long vowel as in sun-shine. Model sunshine: Read sunshine by blending sun | shine. Sun has short u; shine has sh and long i marked by final e. Blend sun-shine into sunshine. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Dale, gone, crumb, blanket, turns, and off; demonstrate that sunshine contains two syllables although the final e is silent. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: Two Windows on Rain
passages.text:
Rain runs ribbons down the pane.
Drip and drop and drip again.
One small window, two small chairs,
Two big thoughts about the stairs.

“The stairs will be wet,” said Miri. “Our picnic is spoiled.”
“The stairs will shine,” said Sol. “We can draw the drops.”
Miri folded the picnic cloth. Sol spread drawing paper on the table. After a while, Miri traced one long drop that had swallowed three little drops. “It is a river now,” she said.
Sol pushed over a pencil. They ate their sandwiches by the window. Miri still wished for the park, but she saved her river picture.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Window-Watching Notes
passages.text:
This passage describes our class observation page. The page has three boxes labeled Time, What I See, and Drawing. A time entry tells when the observation was made. A seeing entry describes a visible detail, such as a round drop on the glass.
A feeling belongs in a separate comment, not in the seeing box. “I feel disappointed” tells a response. “Three drops join into one” tells an observation. Both can matter, but they answer different questions.
The drawing box records shapes and positions. It does not need a beautiful picture; it needs a clear record of what the observer notices.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

explanation: Rhyme can make directions in a poem memorable: sun/run reinforces that the parade is walking, while sign/line connects the display to its arrangement. Kit’s viewpoint begins with excitement about speed. Ana points to a consequence he has overlooked. His later call and waiting show changed behavior, which is stronger evidence than simply calling him nice.

An author’s purpose can be to explain why a plan exists. This passage does not give every step for building a wagon; it explains spacing and pace. Link each reason to the correct choice: turning room supports spaces, while keeping gaps steady supports walking. Broad topic words alone do not identify the exact question the author answers.

A vowel team can stay together inside a longer word: rain-bow. Find the familiar parts, then blend without separating the team. Model rainbow: Read rainbow by blending rain | bow. Rain uses ai for long a; bow uses ow for long o here. Blend the two known parts into rainbow. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Ray, would, need, bowl, beside, and sunrise; keep ai, oa, and ow teams intact. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: The Slow Parade
passages.text:
Step, step, under the sun,
Our small parade is not a run.
Wave the ribbon, lift the sign,
Leave a little space in line.

“Slow is boring,” said Kit, bouncing beside the first wagon. “We should race to the gate.”
“Our paper dragon has a long tail,” said Ana. “If we race, the tail will catch the wheels.”
Kit looked back. Four children held the dragon, and the last child was carefully lifting its tail around a corner. Kit stopped bouncing. At the next turn he called, “Wide turn!” and waited for everyone to pass. The parade moved slowly, but the dragon arrived whole.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Why This Parade Has Spaces
passages.text:
Our classroom parade plan asks each wagon group to leave a space before the next group. This passage explains that choice. A wagon needs room to stop or turn without touching another wagon.
The paper decorations also take up space. A long tail may sweep sideways during a turn. The person carrying it needs room to lift or guide it.
Walking at a steady pace helps the group stay together. Racing would make the gaps change quickly. The plan is about this pretend classroom parade, whose wagons and decorations need careful handling.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Wind’s Reply
passages.text:
“Whoosh,” said the wind to the flag on the pole.
“Flap,” said the flag, “you are making me roll.”
“Whoosh,” said the wind to a hat on a head.
“Stay,” said its owner, “stay here instead!”

Ezra read the wind in a booming voice. Mae read the hat owner sharply, with both hands on her own hat. “The wind sounds proud,” Ezra said.
“Or just busy,” Mae replied. “It does not know about the hat.”
They tried the lines again. This time Ezra made the second whoosh softer. The same words could suggest a playful wind or a careless one, depending on his voice. They kept both readings for their class performance.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: What a Windsock Shows in Our Model
passages.text:
A windsock is a tube of light material with an opening at each end. This description concerns our classroom paper model. A fan moves air toward its wide opening. The narrow end lifts and points away from the fan.
We label the fan AIR SOURCE and draw an arrow from it toward the wide opening. The arrow records the direction used in this model. It does not tell how fast the air moves.
The model helps us describe a direction. It does not show the wind’s feelings. Words such as proud and playful belong to an imagined character, not to a measurement on this diagram.

passages.title: A Tiny Tiger, A Giant Spider
passages.text:
Tiny tiger, tiptoe through,
A paper jungle made for you.
Giant spider, soft and wide,
Leaves a space to step inside.

“That spider is frightening,” said Jo, looking at Ada’s picture. “Its legs cover half the page.”
“It is making a doorway,” Ada replied. “Look at the space beneath the legs.”
Jo traced the open patch with one finger. “I see the doorway. I would still walk around.”
Ada drew a path that went both through and around the spider. They named the picture Two Ways Through the Jungle. Jo read the tiger’s lines cautiously; Ada gave the spider a welcoming voice.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Scale in a Paper Scene
passages.text:
Scale can describe how large one part of a picture is compared with another. This passage answers a question about a made-up paper scene: why does the spider look giant?
The spider stretches across half the page, while the tiger is smaller than a thumb. Their sizes in the picture create the comparison. These paper sizes do not describe the usual sizes of real animals.
A viewer can also compare the path with the figures. A wide space under the spider makes an opening for the paper tiger. Describing that space tells what is drawn; deciding it feels friendly or scary is a viewer’s response.

passages.title: The Quiet Last Line
passages.text:
Cupcake sun and snowflake moon,
Meet upon a paper spoon.
Spin the spoon and let it rest,
Which strange supper tastes the best?

“This poem should be read very fast,” said Ren. “The supper is silly.”
“I want to slow down at the question,” said Pavi. “We need time to imagine it.”
Ren rushed through the four lines. Pavi laughed but could not repeat the last question. They tried again with a little pause before it. This time the class answered with its own impossible foods: cloud soup and pebble pie. Ren kept the quick, playful beginning and let the last line wait for its listeners.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Listening Check
passages.text:
This guide explains how partners can test whether an aloud reading is clear. One partner reads a short passage while the other listens without seeing the page. The listener says what happened or what question was asked.
If an important part was missed, the reader locates that part and rereads it. Changing pace or grouping words may help. Speaking louder is not the answer to every problem.
The partners then exchange roles. The purpose is understanding, not winning a speed contest. A clear reading keeps the printed words accurate while making their connections easy to hear.

explanation: Words tell the sequence: the door strikes a box, Tari tests it, and the children move the obstruction. The supplied plan represents the final arrangement, so it adds locations that should not be mistaken for the beginning. Combine time information from the prose with place information from the plan. This is a text-described illustration; students can sketch it before explaining what it contributes.

Match each reason to its own point. Empty space supports the doorway rule; labels support finding the correct box. Swapping the reasons makes weak explanations even though both reasons appear in the text. The diagram and glossary clarify swing as movement around a hinge, not playground equipment. Read the key and caption before answering a spatial question.

The prefix un- can mean not or reverse an action. Read the base, add un, and test the meaning in the sentence. Model unsafe: Read unsafe by blending un | safe. Read safe with long a, then add un, pronounced like the start of under. Unsafe means not safe. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Nia, knot (silent k), string, asks, again, and each; map the unexpected silent k explicitly. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. passages.title: The Door That Could Open
passages.text:
Tari arranged boxes for a pretend shop. She put a tall box near the back wall and a low counter in front. When Bo tried to enter, the door struck a box and stopped. Tari looked annoyed until Bo invited her to try it herself. She pushed the door and felt the same bump.
They moved the small box to the back wall. Now the door opened fully, and Bo carried the first pretend purchase through. Tari made a paper plan so the next shopkeeper would know why the entrance needed space.
Picture plan, viewed from above after the move:
BACK WALL: [tall box] [small box]
MIDDLE: [low counter]
FRONT: clear space beside the inward-opening DOOR
Caption: The boxes have moved away from the door’s swing.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Leave Room to Open
passages.text:
Point 1: Keep a model shop doorway clear. Reason: An inward-opening door needs an empty area through which to swing.
Point 2: Put labels on the storage boxes. Reason: A label lets a shopkeeper choose a box without opening every lid. These two reasons solve different problems.
Diagram key: D = closed door; curved arrow = the path of its opening edge. Text diagram: FRONT WALL — D; curved arrow leads inward into EMPTY SPACE. A box is shown beyond that empty space, against the BACK WALL.
Glossary: swing—the curved movement of a door around its hinge.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Path Through the Display
passages.text:
The class built a paper town on a table. Remy placed a tower in the middle of the main street. “Everyone will see it,” he said. But when Jo moved a toy bus along the drawn road, the tower blocked its route. Remy slid the tower to the square beside the street. Jo drove the bus past, then stopped where its passengers could pretend to visit.
Remy added a small sign pointing from the bus stop to the tower. The tower was still easy to find, and now the road worked too.
Map after the change: START → MAIN STREET → BUS STOP → END. TOWER SQUARE lies beside BUS STOP, reached by a short side path. Caption: The tower is beside the route, not on it.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Signs for a Tabletop Town
passages.text:
A route is a path followed from one place to another. The main route in our town model should stay open because the toy bus must travel along it. A side path can connect an important building to that route.
Signs should point toward their destinations because a reader uses the arrow to choose a direction. A large letter on a sign does not fix an arrow pointing the wrong way.
Diagram: BUS STOP → SIDE PATH → TOWER. Caption: Follow the arrow from the stop, along the side path, to the tower. The arrow gives direction; it does not tell distance.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

explanation: The prose supplies a small mistake, a helpful response, and the effect on later users. The illustration description adds an arrangement and a tray not explained in the story’s action. The author links sorting to finding a size and the tray to collecting drips. These are separate points with separate reasons. The diagram’s arrows label nested parts; the caption warns that they are not time-order arrows. A familiar symbol can serve different purposes in different texts, so a reader must check the local key or caption before interpreting it.

Preteach classroom, lids, Fran, clear, writes, their, and too; explain that -ful has one l even though full has two. passages.title: The Helpful Shelf
passages.text:
Nell could never find a short paintbrush in the crowded art cup. She tipped out every brush and sorted them by size. Her partner Luis wrote labels for three jars. Nell began putting the longest brushes into the jar marked SHORT. Luis did not grab them. He pointed at the word, then at the shortest jar. Nell laughed and switched the brushes.
When another class came to paint, Nell showed them the shelf. She was proud of the labels, but prouder that nobody needed to dump a cup onto the table.
Illustration description: Three jars stand left to right: SHORT, MEDIUM, LONG. Each contains brushes of matching length. A shallow tray sits beneath all three. Caption: The tray catches drips beneath the sorted brushes.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Two Jobs on One Art Shelf
passages.text:
Sort brushes by length so a painter can find a useful size without emptying every jar. Label each jar with a length word. The labels identify the groups even when a jar is nearly empty.
Use a shallow tray under the jars to collect drips. The tray’s rim is a raised edge. Water inside the rim stays off the shelf until the tray is emptied.
Diagram labels: BRUSH → JAR → TRAY. The jar stands inside the tray’s raised RIM. Caption: The arrows name nested parts, not a sequence of washing steps.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Helpful Note
passages.text: A helpful note is on the classroom box. It says, “Put the lids here.” Fran reads it and puts a lid in. She feels thankful for the clear words. Then Fran writes a new note for the pens. Her pal can find their spot, too.

passages.title: Cloudless on One Side
passages.text:
Gus drew a sky for the class weather-play stage. One side was filled with clouds; the other was bright and empty. “You forgot half the sky,” said Tia. Gus shook his head. He placed a paper window in front of the picture and slid the sky behind it. First the window showed clouds, then clear blue.
Tia tried moving it too fast. The picture caught on the frame. Together they added a handle below the picture where it would not cover the window. Tia wrote CLEAR on one end and CLOUDY on the other. Their tiny stage could now change weather with one careful slide.
Stage plan: [CLOUDY end: three cloud shapes]—[CLEAR end: no cloud shapes]. HANDLE extends below; WINDOW shows only one end at a time.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Moving Backdrop
passages.text:
A backdrop is a picture behind a stage scene. In this model, a strip slides behind a window-shaped opening. The window hides the rest of the strip so the audience sees only the chosen scene.
Point: Put the handle below the visible picture. Reason: A hand can then move the strip without covering the scene.
Point: Mark the two ends clearly. Reason: The operator can choose the needed scene without sliding back and forth to search.
Key for the stage plan: three cloud shapes = cloudy scene; no cloud shapes = clear scene. These symbols describe this paper model, not a weather measurement.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Cloudless Day
passages.text: On a cloudless day, Gus takes a red kite to the field. The kite string has a knot. Gus is not helpless: he can ask for help. His aunt loosens the knot. Gus thanks her and holds the string with care. The kite lifts into the sky.

passages.title: The Taller Welcome
passages.text:
A class made three block towers for a welcome display. Beth built the tallest tower in front. When guests stood at the door, they could see only its bright flag. The two shorter towers disappeared behind it. Beth stepped to the door and looked. “I built a wall,” she said.
She moved the tallest tower to the back and set the shorter ones in front, leaving space between them. All three flags appeared. Beth drew a plan for rebuilding the display after cleanup. She also wrote, “Check from the guest’s place.”
Front-view plan after the move: short tower—2 blocks; medium tower—3 blocks; tall tower behind the gap—5 blocks. Caption: The tallest tower stands at the back so it does not hide the shorter towers.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: What Our Display Chart Shows
passages.text:
The class chart records the blocks used in three towers: Short—2; Medium—3; Tall—5. Each number counts blocks, not height in inches. If blocks differed in size, the count alone would not give exact height.
The display planner recommends putting a taller object behind shorter objects. The stated reason is visibility: viewers should be able to see each object.
A second recommendation is leaving room between objects. Its reason is access: a hand can reach one tower without knocking another. The chart lists quantities; the paragraphs explain the planner’s reasons.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Taller Tower
passages.text: Beth builds a tall block tower. Remy builds a taller one. Lee tries to build the tallest tower, but it tips. Lee starts with a wider base. This time the tower stays up. The friends compare their towers without knocking them down.

explanation: A diagram can show the finished design while the prose explains how it came about. The illustration’s MONDAY card confirms the eventual change without showing Omar’s earlier worry. The pocket and envelope serve separate jobs: changing and storing. Combine these details with the ending to explain why Omar responds differently when the schedule changes.

The author supports two points with practical reasons. A removable date saves replacing the whole sign, while grouped cards make finding a replacement easier. The sequence arrows here really do show order, unlike the nested-part diagram earlier in the unit. The caption explains why reading the entire sign remains necessary after changing only one card.

Read a base with its added parts in order. A prefix and suffix can both change meaning, as un-help-ful means not helpful. Model unhelpful: Read unhelpful by blending un | help | ful. Read help, add ful to make helpful, then add un. Unhelpful means not helpful; all three parts remain in the pronunciation. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach reusable, puppet, unclear, would, slowly, and wipe; model reusable as re-use-able for access rather than testing an untaught ending. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. passages.title: The Sign That Could Change
passages.text:
Omar wrote FRIDAY SHOW on a bright sign. The class cheered, but the teacher said the show might move to Monday. Omar reached for a fresh sheet. Nia stopped him and pointed to the empty space below SHOW. “Could the day be a separate card?” she asked.
They covered FRIDAY with a blank strip, attached a small pocket below SHOW, and slipped a day card into it. The sign could now change without being thrown away. Omar made two more cards and kept them in an envelope behind the sign. When the day changed, he smiled instead of reaching for new paper.
Illustration description: The main sign reads SHOW. A pocket below holds MONDAY. Behind it is an envelope marked DAY CARDS. Caption: The title stays; the day card can be replaced.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Reusable Notice
passages.text:
Point: Keep the event name on a main sign and put the date on a removable card. Reason: A changed date then requires one small replacement rather than a whole new sign.
Point: Store unused cards together. Reason: The correct card can be found when needed.
Sequence diagram: REMOVE OLD DAY → SELECT NEW DAY → SLIDE NEW DAY INTO POCKET → READ WHOLE SIGN. Caption: The final reading checks that the new day and event title make sense together.
Glossary: reusable—able to be used again; removable—able to be taken away.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: A class makes a sign for a playful puppet show. The sign has a blank space for the day. The class can reuse it. An unclear note would be unhelpful, so they write slowly. After the show, they wipe the day away and save the sign.

explanation: Compare the event shared by both versions before noting changes. Both mice free a lion by gnawing rope, but one lion is tied to a tree while the other is tied to the ground. Townsend’s mouse recognizes the roar; Jacobs’s mouse happens to pass. Those details change how the rescue begins without changing the central reversal of a powerful animal needing a small one. These are two published English tellings in the Aesop tradition, not a claim that either is the universal original. The adult reads both and explains older vocabulary before comparison; students are not expected to decode the historical prose independently.

The two help-station texts share the point that help should fit the job. The first emphasizes tools and storage; the second emphasizes a partner’s request and limited role. Shared topic does not mean identical information. Attribute an example to its source and use the exact reason each source provides rather than importing a fable’s moral as a workshop fact.

passages.title: The Lion and the Mouse — Jacobs
passages.text:
Once when a Lion was asleep a little Mouse began running up and down upon him; this soon wakened the Lion, who placed his huge paw upon him, and opened his big jaws to swallow him. “Pardon, O King,” cried the little Mouse: “forgive me this time, I shall never forget it: who knows but what I may be able to do you a turn some of these days?” The Lion was so tickled at the idea of the Mouse being able to help him, that he lifted up his paw and let him go. Some time after the Lion was caught in a trap, and the hunters who desired to carry him alive to the King, tied him to a tree while they went in search of a waggon to carry him on. Just then the little Mouse happened to pass by, and seeing the sad plight in which the Lion was, went up to him and soon gnawed away the ropes that bound the King of the Beasts. “Was I not right?” said the little Mouse.

Little friends may prove great friends.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894), “The Lion and the Mouse.” Public domain in the USA. Text from Project Gutenberg; whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Help Station: Finding a Tool
passages.text:
In our class model workshop, a help station holds a ruler, a clip, and a large-handled magnifier. A child chooses a tool for a particular job. The ruler helps compare lengths; the clip holds paper together; the magnifier helps a viewer inspect a small mark.
The station’s sign says, “Choose by the job, not by size.” A large tool is not automatically the right one. Put each tool back so another classmate can find it.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Bread for the Trip
passages.text: Leah has bread and jam in a bag. Her team will take a short trip. She reads the list at the top of the page. Each child brings one snack. Leah checks her bag, then helps a friend read the list. They are ready to go.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Lion and the Mouse — Townsend
passages.text:
A LION was awakened from sleep by a Mouse running over his face. Rising up angrily, he caught him and was about to kill him, when the Mouse piteously entreated, saying: “If you would only spare my life, I would be sure to repay your kindness.” The Lion laughed and let him go. It happened shortly after this that the Lion was caught by some hunters, who bound him by strong ropes to the ground. The Mouse, recognizing his roar, came and gnawed the rope with his teeth, and set him free, exclaiming:

“You ridiculed the idea of my ever being able to help you, not expecting to receive from me any repayment of your favour; now you know that it is possible for even a Mouse to confer benefits on a Lion.”
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; George Fyler Townsend, Three hundred Aesop’s fables, Project Gutenberg edition released 2008, “The Lion and the Mouse.” Historical translation; public domain in the USA. Whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Help Station: Asking a Partner
passages.text:
Our workshop partners begin by naming the job that is difficult. One might ask, “Can you hold this paper while I draw?” The other can agree, suggest a tool, or explain what help is possible.
Being helpful does not mean doing everything for another person. A partner may hold one edge while the maker completes the drawing. The plan matches the help to the job and gives both people a role.

explanation: Both versions contain a boastful hare, a race, a sleeping hare, and a winning tortoise. Townsend names the Fox as course chooser and describes the tortoise resting after finishing; Jacobs gives more spoken challenge and ends with the tortoise’s line. Keep those details with the right version. A fable lesson about persistence should not become a blanket rule that every pause or rest is bad. These are two published English tellings in the Aesop tradition, not a claim that either is the universal original. The adult reads both and explains older vocabulary before comparison; students are not expected to decode the historical prose independently.

The practice texts both describe routines that support understanding, but one focuses on regular short practice and the other on useful pauses and recording help. Their details prevent an overbroad transfer from the racing fable. A real learner may need a pause even though the hare’s nap contributes to his fictional loss. Compare the texts’ actual points before drawing a conclusion.

Ow can say long o in grow or /ow/ in brown. Try known pronunciations only after attending to all the letters. Model bowl: Read bowl by blending b | ow | l. Ow says long o in bowl. Add /b/ before the vowel and /l/ after it; say the word as one syllable. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach flower, water, forever, cut, everyone, yellow, and clown; contrast brown and bowl side by side. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: The Hare and the Tortoise — Jacobs
passages.text:
The Hare was once boasting of his speed before the other animals. “I have never yet been beaten,” said he, “when I put forth my full speed. I challenge any one here to race with me.”

The Tortoise said quietly, “I accept your challenge.”

“That is a good joke,” said the Hare; “I could dance round you all the way.”

“Keep your boasting till you’ve beaten,” answered the Tortoise. “Shall we race?”

So a course was fixed and a start was made. The Hare darted almost out of sight at once, but soon stopped and, to show his contempt for the Tortoise, lay down to have a nap. The Tortoise plodded on and plodded on, and when the Hare awoke from his nap, he saw the Tortoise just near the winning-post and could not run up in time to save the race. Then said the Tortoise:

“Plodding wins the race.”
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894), “The Hare and the Tortoise.” Public domain in the USA. Text from Project Gutenberg; whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Practice Log: Steady Work
passages.text:
Our class practice log gives each reader a short, manageable part to rehearse. The reader marks an accurate first try, a word to repair, and a second try. The log values improvement in a chosen part rather than the greatest number of pages.
A regular brief practice time helps the reader return to the same goal. The log does not say that slow reading is always better; accurate understanding remains the aim.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Brown Bowl
passages.text: A brown bowl sits low on the shelf. Ben takes it down. He puts a flower in water in the bowl. The flower will not grow there forever; it is a cut flower for the table. Ben sets it on the table where everyone can see it.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Hare and the Tortoise — Townsend
passages.text:
A HARE one day ridiculed the short feet and slow pace of the Tortoise, who replied, laughing: “Though you be swift as the wind, I will beat you in a race.” The Hare, believing her assertion to be simply impossible, assented to the proposal; and they agreed that the Fox should choose the course and fix the goal. On the day appointed for the race the two started together. The Tortoise never for a moment stopped, but went on with a slow but steady pace straight to the end of the course. The Hare, lying down by the wayside, fell fast asleep. At last waking up, and moving as fast as he could, he saw the Tortoise had reached the goal, and was comfortably dozing after her fatigue.

Slow but steady wins the race.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; George Fyler Townsend, Three hundred Aesop’s fables, Project Gutenberg edition released 2008, “The Hare and the Tortoise.” Historical translation; public domain in the USA. Whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Practice Log: Useful Rest
passages.text:
In our class reading routine, a pause can be useful. A reader may stop to ask about an unfamiliar word, think about a sentence, or rest a tired voice. The reader then returns to the passage.
A partner records the help given during the pause. A supported reading should not be described as an unaided first try. The record helps the teacher choose the next lesson rather than compare children as winners and losers.

passages.title: The Crow and the Pitcher — Jacobs
passages.text:
A Crow, half-dead with thirst, came upon a Pitcher which had once been full of water; but when the Crow put its beak into the mouth of the Pitcher he found that only very little water was left in it, and that he could not reach far enough down to get at it. He tried, and he tried, but at last had to give up in despair. Then a thought came to him, and he took a pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. At last, at last, he saw the water mount up near him, and after casting in a few more pebbles he was able to quench his thirst and save his life.

Little by little does the trick.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894), “The Crow and the Pitcher.” Public domain in the USA. Text from Project Gutenberg; whitespace normalized.

passages.title: A Water-Level Model
passages.text:
For this adult-led classroom model, a clear cup stands in a tray with a low water level. An adult marks the starting line and adds clean stones one at a time. The class observes whether the water line changes. The cup is not drinking water, and the stones are handled by the adult.
The purpose is to compare a starting level with later levels. A visible mark makes the comparison easier than remembering the first line.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Good Spoon
passages.text: A wood spoon is in the toy kitchen. Liv thinks it could stir a pot of pretend soup. Her friend brings a bowl. They take turns serving the soup to dolls. No one eats it. At the end, they put the wood spoon back on its hook.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Crow and the Pitcher — Townsend
passages.text:
A CROW perishing with thirst saw a pitcher, and hoping to find water, flew to it with delight. When he reached it, he discovered to his grief that it contained so little water that he could not possibly get at it. He tried everything he could think of to reach the water, but all his efforts were in vain. At last he collected as many stones as he could carry and dropped them one by one with his beak into the pitcher, until he brought the water within his reach and thus saved his life.

Necessity is the mother of invention.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; George Fyler Townsend, Three hundred Aesop’s fables, Project Gutenberg edition released 2008, “The Crow and the Pitcher.” Historical translation; public domain in the USA. Whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Recording the Same Model
passages.text:
A recording sheet for the water-level model has three columns: Stones Added, Water-Line Drawing, and Notes. After each stone, a recorder draws the new water line. A note can say higher, unchanged, or spilled if that is what was observed.
The sheet records observations, not a promised result. If water spills, record the spill because it changes what remains in the cup. Do not quietly replace a surprising observation with the result someone expected.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

explanation: A character’s statement is not automatically a narrator-confirmed fact. Both foxes call unreachable grapes sour after failing to get them. Townsend’s narrator first calls them ripe and later says the fox hides disappointment; Jacobs describes repeated jumps and a proud departure. The first teaches a claim limit; the second records questions that remain open. A statement can be unsupported without being proven false. passages.title: The Fox and the Grapes — Jacobs
passages.text:
One hot summer’s day a Fox was strolling through an orchard till he came to a bunch of Grapes just ripening on a vine which had been trained over a lofty branch. “Just the thing to quench my thirst,” quoth he. Drawing back a few paces, he took a run and a jump, and just missed the bunch. Turning round again with a One, Two, Three, he jumped up, but with no greater success. Again and again he tried after the tempting morsel, but at last had to give it up, and walked away with his nose in the air, saying: “I am sure they are sour.”

It is easy to despise what you cannot get.

passages.title: Observation Before a Claim
passages.text:
Our class sorts paper fruit pictures by visible color. A card may show purple grapes, a green apple, or a yellow pear. A recorder writes only colors actually shown. The pictures do not provide flavor, smell, or ripeness.
When a classmate says, “That purple fruit must be sweet,” the recorder asks what evidence is available. The picture supports purple, but it does not establish sweet. This activity separates a visible feature from an unsupported claim.

passages.title: What the Sign Said
passages.text: A sign said, “Walk this way.” The arrow pointed left. Tess went left and found the room. A new sign says, “Please knock.” Tess knocked, and a voice called, “Come in!” Tess read each sign again before she went home.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Fox and the Grapes — Townsend
passages.text: A FAMISHED FOX saw some clusters of ripe black grapes hanging from a trellised vine. She resorted to all her tricks to get at them, but wearied herself in vain, for she could not reach them. At last she turned away, hiding her disappointment and saying: “The Grapes are sour, and not ripe as I thought.”

passages.title: Questions We Cannot Answer Yet
passages.text:
A question board keeps track of information our fruit-picture activity does not supply. Students can post “How does it taste?” or “Where did it grow?” The board marks those questions NOT SHOWN.
Not shown does not mean false. It means the class needs another suitable source or observation to answer. Guessing confidently would hide the information gap. Naming the gap makes a later investigation more useful.

passages.title: The Wind and the Sun — Jacobs
passages.text:
The Wind and the Sun were disputing which was the stronger. Suddenly they saw a traveller coming down the road, and the Sun said: “I see a way to decide our dispute. Whichever of us can cause that traveller to take off his cloak shall be regarded as the stronger. You begin.” So the Sun retired behind a cloud, and the Wind began to blow as hard as it could upon the traveller. But the harder he blew the more closely did the traveller wrap his cloak round him, till at last the Wind had to give up in despair. Then the Sun came out and shone in all his glory upon the traveller, who soon found it too hot to walk with his cloak on.

Kindness effects more than severity.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894), “The Wind and the Sun.” Public domain in the USA. Text from Project Gutenberg; whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Inviting a Partner
passages.text:
Our classroom game guide recommends explaining an invitation instead of pulling someone into a game. Say what the game involves and ask whether the person wants a turn. A clear explanation helps the person make a choice.
The guide does not promise every invitation will be accepted. A classmate may prefer another activity. Respecting that answer keeps the invitation from becoming pressure.

passages.title: A Gift to Give
passages.text: I have a little gift to give. It is a card for my friend. I drew a bright sun on the front. Inside I wrote, “I love our games.” My friend gave me a grin and set the card on a shelf. I felt glad.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Wind and the Sun — Townsend
passages.text:
THE NORTH WIND and the Sun disputed as to which was the most powerful, and agreed that he should be declared the victor who could first strip a wayfaring man of his clothes. The North Wind first tried his power and blew with all his might, but the keener his blasts, the closer the Traveler wrapped his cloak around him, until at last, resigning all hope of victory, the Wind called upon the Sun to see what he could do. The Sun suddenly shone out with all his warmth. The Traveler no sooner felt his genial rays than he took off one garment after another, and at last, fairly overcome with heat, undressed and bathed in a stream that lay in his path.

Persuasion is better than Force.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; George Fyler Townsend, Three hundred Aesop’s fables, Project Gutenberg edition released 2008, “The North Wind and the Sun.” Historical translation; public domain in the USA. Whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Explaining a Classroom Choice
passages.text:
When our class chooses a group activity, a speaker gives a proposal and a reason. “Choose drawing because we have space and supplies” is one example. Another student may offer a different proposal with a reason.
The teacher records the reasons so the class can compare them. Loudness alone does not show that an idea fits the situation. The aim is to understand the choices, not to reward the most forceful voice.

passages.title: The Fox and the Crow — Jacobs
passages.text:
A Fox once saw a Crow fly off with a piece of cheese in its beak and settle on a branch of a tree. “That’s for me, as I am a Fox,” said Master Reynard, and he walked up to the foot of the tree. “Good-day, Mistress Crow,” he cried. “How well you are looking to-day: how glossy your feathers; how bright your eye. I feel sure your voice must surpass that of other birds, just as your figure does; let me hear but one song from you that I may greet you as the Queen of Birds.” The Crow lifted up her head and began to caw her best, but the moment she opened her mouth the piece of cheese fell to the ground, only to be snapped up by Master Fox. “That will do,” said he. “That was all I wanted. In exchange for your cheese I will give you a piece of advice for the future—

“Do not trust flatterers.”

The Flatter doth rob by stealth, His victim, both of Wit and Wealth.
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; Joseph Jacobs, The Fables of Aesop (1894), “The Fox and the Crow.” Public domain in the USA. Text from Project Gutenberg; whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Specific Helpful Feedback
passages.text:
Our art partners give feedback that names a visible detail. “Your label is easy to read because the letters have space” tells the maker what worked. “Everything is perfect” gives little information about a particular choice.
Helpful feedback can include a question: “Could the arrow point closer to the doorway?” The purpose is to improve the work while leaving decisions with its maker. It is not a promise that every suggestion must be used.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Who Has Two?
passages.text: “Who has two red cubes?” asks Kit. I have one, and Val has one. We put them side by side. Now we have two. Kit gives us a blue cube as well. We count once more. The group has three cubes in all.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Fox and the Crow — Townsend
passages.text: A CROW having stolen a bit of meat, perched in a tree and held it in her beak. A Fox, seeing this, longed to possess the meat himself, and by a wily stratagem succeeded. “How handsome is the Crow,” he exclaimed, “in the beauty of her shape and in the fairness of her complexion! Oh, if her voice were only equal to her beauty, she would deservedly be considered the Queen of Birds!” This he said deceitfully; but the Crow, anxious to refute the reflection cast upon her voice, set up a loud caw and dropped the flesh. The Fox quickly picked it up, and thus addressed the Crow: “My good Crow, your voice is right enough, but your wit is wanting.”
passages.attribution: Aesop tradition; George Fyler Townsend, Three hundred Aesop’s fables, Project Gutenberg edition released 2008, “The Fox and the Crow.” Historical translation; public domain in the USA. Whitespace normalized.

passages.title: Check the Purpose of a Message
passages.text:
Our classroom message check asks two questions: What does the speaker say, and what does the speaker want to happen? A message may praise a picture, request a turn, or explain a rule. The same pleasant tone can accompany different purposes.
Look for actions as well as words. If someone praises your turn-taking only when asking to cut ahead, ask about the request itself. A kind-sounding statement is not evidence that every requested action is fair.

weeks.objective: Infer a fable’s lesson and compare a changed ending. Vowel-team transfer

connection.before: Build on week 30: Attribute shared and unique details in paired tales and information.
connection.after: Next week, apply this evidence work to recount a tale and explain how accurate details affect its lesson; word work moves to two-syllable transfer.

days: Day 1: Introduce vowel-team transfer. Model sunbeam; blend fresh words with feedback. Adult reads The Otter’s Shining Stone and A Different Ending for Otter; discuss the worked evidence example.
Day 2: Revisit the story for infer a fable’s lesson and compare a changed ending; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read A Sunbeam Map independently after word preparation.

explanation: The fable’s lesson grows from Otter’s mistaken explanation and her later observation. More shine would not open the path. Moving the stone beside the door meets two needs, and the scene description confirms that arrangement. The alternate ending solves only the blocked path. Compare consequences before deciding which ending better supports thoughtful sharing; reasonable preferences still need details.

The main information text develops two connected goals across three paragraphs. The second text adds a third concern, connecting labels with objects, while sharing the visitor-centered viewpoint. Distinguish the whole topic of display planning from the narrower second-paragraph focus on marking a route. These supplied texts practice synthesis but do not certify reading across the full grades 2–3 complexity band.

Review long-vowel teams and less regular alternatives, choosing the pronunciation that matches both the letters and the known spoken word. Model sunbeam: Read sunbeam by blending sun | beam. Sun is a short-u closed syllable; beam has ea for long e. Blend sun-beam to name a beam of sunlight. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Hana, marks, patch, compare, natural, and later; adult supplies any unfamiliar map vocabulary. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately.
