passages.title: The Otter’s Shining Stone
passages.text:
Otter found a shining stone beside the stream. She wanted every visitor to admire it, so she put it on the narrow path to her door. Duck tripped beside it and flapped into the reeds. Otter polished the stone again. “Perhaps it was not shiny enough,” she said.
Beaver stopped before reaching the stone. “I can see it very well,” he said. “I cannot pass it.” Otter looked from the stone to the path and finally understood. She rolled the stone onto a broad stump beside the entrance. Duck returned and admired its blue stripe. Otter discovered that a treasure could be seen without standing in everyone’s way.
Scene description: After the move, the stump and stone are left of the doorway. The path runs straight to the door with no stone on it.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Display Has Two Jobs
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: Our classroom display plan asks two questions: Can visitors see the objects, and can visitors move through the space? A bright object in a doorway may be visible while blocking the route.
Paragraph 2: The class marks an open route on a paper plan before placing display stands. The stands go beside that route. A partner traces the route with a finger to check for blocked places.
Paragraph 3: After arranging the stands, the class checks the view from the entrance. A successful plan considers movement and visibility together.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Sunbeam Map
passages.text: A sunbeam falls on the rug. Hana marks its spot on a paper map of the room. Later, the bright patch is in a new place. Hana marks that spot too. She does not move the rug. She wants to compare what she sees at two times.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Different Ending for Otter
passages.text: Original alternate ending: After Beaver says he cannot pass, Otter pushes the stone into a deep, closed chest. The path becomes clear, but no visitor can see the blue stripe. Duck arrives and asks about the famous stone. Otter says, “I hid it so nobody would trip.” Beaver suggests opening the chest in a place beside the path. Otter has solved one problem but still needs a way to share her treasure.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Labels at the Display
passages.text: A label should sit near the object it names so a visitor can connect them. In our display plan, a label placed far away could seem to name a different object. Read the label from the visitor’s standing place. This check concerns clear identification, while the route check concerns movement. Both help a visitor use the display.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

weeks.title: Two Messages for Mouse
weeks.objective: Recount a tale and explain how accurate details affect its lesson. Two-syllable transfer

connection.before: Build on week 31: Infer a fable’s lesson and compare a changed ending.
connection.after: Next week, apply this evidence work to support a lesson with choices and compare informational procedures; word work moves to affix transfer.

days: Day 1: Introduce two-syllable transfer. Model mailbox; blend fresh words with feedback. Adult reads Two Messages for Mouse and Mouse Keeps the Exact Message; discuss the worked evidence example.
Day 2: Revisit the story for recount a tale and explain how accurate details affect its lesson; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read The Mailbox Model independently after word preparation.
Day 3: Adult reads Our Message Slip and A Reply Slip; examine the organization and vocabulary in each. Connect its details to the story without treating fiction as factual evidence.
Day 4: Use worksheet B, repair printed-word errors, and reread The Mailbox Model with meaningful phrases; record accuracy and support, not a speed race.
Day 5: Select worksheet C for transfer. Ask for a new text-supported oral explanation and hear an individual rereading; reteach observed word patterns.
explanation: A recount must preserve details that cause the problem. Biggest tree and dark are not harmless synonyms for willow and sunset. Mouse’s wish to sound important changes the plan. The alternate version models a different response to uncertainty: returning to check. Both endings value accuracy, but one repairs a mistake after harm and the other prevents the confusion.

The message-slip paragraphs develop content, checking, and handling uncertainty. The companion adds a receiver’s role. Their shared goal is a common understanding, but they assign checks to different people. Read back and reply are related methods, not identical steps. Use the supplied invitation details to explain why exact time and place words matter.

Recognize familiar syllables, blend them, and confirm the whole word without replacing it with a guessed word of similar shape. Model mailbox: Read mailbox by blending mail | box. Mail has ai for long a and box has short o; x supplies /ks/. Blend mail-box to name the container for mail. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Ravi, Mina, slot, both, explain, family, and basket; review ai and final-e patterns. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

passages.title: Two Messages for Mouse
passages.text:
Mouse promised to carry an invitation from the pond to the meadow. “At sunset, beside the willow,” said Frog. Mouse repeated the message and hurried away. On the path, he met Finch, who asked about the party. Mouse wanted to sound important. “At the biggest tree, when the sky is dark,” he announced.
Finch flew to the old oak after nightfall. Nobody was there. Meanwhile, Frog waited by the willow as the sun disappeared. The next morning Mouse heard what had happened. He drew a willow on a leaf and asked Frog to check the words beneath it: SUNSET, WILLOW. Then he delivered the corrected message and admitted his mistake. The next gathering began with everyone in the same place.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Our Message Slip
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: A classroom message slip records an event, a time, and a place. The writer uses specific words so another person can act on the message. “Later near a tree” is less useful than a named time and tree.
Paragraph 2: The writer reads the slip back to the person who supplied the message. This check can reveal a changed word or missing detail before delivery.
Paragraph 3: If a detail remains uncertain, the writer marks it for checking instead of making it up. The aim is a trustworthy message, not an impressive-sounding one.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Mailbox Model
passages.text: A class makes a mailbox from a box. The lid has a slot for notes. Ravi writes a note to Mina. She reads it and writes back. At sunset, Ravi takes both notes home. He can explain how the class mailbox works to his family.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Mouse Keeps the Exact Message
passages.text: Original alternate version: Mouse carries Frog’s invitation but forgets whether the meeting is at sunset or after dark. He stops rather than adding a grander phrase. He returns to Frog, checks the time, and asks for a leaf note. Finch receives the message later than expected, but it names sunset and the willow correctly. Mouse feels less impressive and more useful.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Reply Slip
passages.text: A reply slip lets the receiver confirm a message. The receiver can write “I will meet you by the willow at sunset” or ask “Which tree?” The reply is not a replacement for a clear original message. It is another chance to discover whether both people understand the same plan.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

weeks.title: The Beaver’s Borrowed Basket
weeks.objective: Support a lesson with choices and compare informational procedures. Affix transfer

connection.before: Build on week 32: Recount a tale and explain how accurate details affect its lesson.
connection.after: Next week, apply this evidence work to explain a character’s response and synthesize two related accounts; word work moves to irregular words in context.

days: Day 1: Introduce affix transfer. Model carefully; blend fresh words with feedback. Adult reads The Beaver’s Borrowed Basket and The Hidden Repair; discuss the worked evidence example. Begin the adult read-aloud of The Elves and the Shoemaker, pausing to explain the listed older words.
Day 2: Revisit the story for support a lesson with choices and compare informational procedures; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read The Careful Helper independently after word preparation.
Day 3: Adult reads Borrowing Classroom Materials and A Return Card; examine the organization and vocabulary in each. Connect its details to the story without treating fiction as factual evidence.

Day 4: Use worksheet B, repair printed-word errors, and reread The Careful Helper with meaningful phrases; record accuracy and support, not a speed race. Finish The Elves and the Shoemaker and use the folktale extension questions to recount and compare its lesson.
Day 5: Select worksheet C for transfer. Ask for a new text-supported oral explanation and hear an individual rereading; reteach observed word patterns.
explanation: Beaver’s difficulty begins before the knot slips: he fails to inspect the borrowed basket. His honest explanation leads to a repair and a clearer future routine. The alternate ending shows why meeting a time promise alone may not be enough. Compare actions without assuming that a hidden problem disappears because the object looks neat.

The three information paragraphs organize care by time: before borrowing, during use, and on return. The return card supports only one part of that larger process. Its labels capture condition and location, but writing a note does not physically fix a loose part. Readers should connect the procedure’s steps and preserve the limits of each tool.

Find a familiar base and read all added parts; use prefix and suffix meanings as checks, not as substitutes for decoding. Model carefully: Read carefully by blending care | ful | ly. Read care, add the unstressed -ful ending, then -ly pronounced /lee/. Carefully means in a careful way. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach Owen, chair, carefully, classmate, together, and useful; model -ly meaning in a careful way. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

Read-aloud folktale extension: This supplied Grimm tale adds a longer traditional story to the original basket fable. Read it over two sessions if useful. Explain cobbler (shoemaker), betimes (early), wights (imagined beings), waistcoat (vest), and pantaloons (trousers). The little helpers belong to a fairy tale, and the narrator’s references to prayer describe this telling’s characters. Trace need, hidden help, discovery, and grateful response. A lesson about returning kindness should be supported by the couple’s clothing gifts, not treated as a promise that magic rewards every hardworking person.

passages.title: The Beaver’s Borrowed Basket
passages.text:
Beaver borrowed Squirrel’s basket to carry reeds. “Bring it back before the evening meal,” Squirrel said. Beaver nodded but did not look inside. At the stream he found a loose handle. He tied it with grass and carried his load. By evening the grass knot had slipped.
Beaver could have returned the basket quietly. Instead he showed Squirrel the loose handle and explained his repair. Squirrel fetched a strong cord, and together they fastened it. “Next time, tell me before carrying the load,” she said. Beaver drew a tiny basket on his work card with three words: CHECK, ASK, RETURN. His promise now included paying attention to the thing he borrowed.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Borrowing Classroom Materials
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: Before borrowing a class tool, inspect it with the person responsible for it. Name any missing or loose part. This check establishes its condition before use.
Paragraph 2: Agree on the return place and time. Keep any small parts together in a tray while working so they are not lost.
Paragraph 3: On return, report changes or problems. An honest report helps the next user make a suitable plan. Returning on time is one part of care, but not the only part.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Careful Helper
passages.text: Owen will refill the class pencil cup. He checks the floor first. A pencil is under a chair. Owen picks it up carefully and puts it in the cup. He does not want a classmate to step on it. The cup is useful when pencils stay together.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Hidden Repair
passages.text: Original alternate ending: Beaver wraps the slipping grass knot in a leaf so it looks neat. He returns the basket without mentioning the handle. When Squirrel lifts it, she sees the loose join and must stop to repair it. Beaver has met the return time but has not supplied information the owner needs. The next morning he comes back to explain what happened.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Return Card
passages.text: A return card has spaces for Item, Where Returned, and Condition. A note such as “one handle is loose” gives more useful information than “fine” when a problem exists. The card supports the spoken report; it does not repair the tool. Someone responsible for the material still decides what to do next.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Elves and the Shoemaker
passages.text:
There was once a shoemaker, who worked very hard and was very honest: but still he could not earn enough to live upon; and at last all he had in the world was gone, save just leather enough to make one pair of shoes.

Then he cut his leather out, all ready to make up the next day, meaning to rise early in the morning to his work. His conscience was clear and his heart light amidst all his troubles; so he went peaceably to bed, left all his cares to Heaven, and soon fell asleep. In the morning after he had said his prayers, he sat himself down to his work; when, to his great wonder, there stood the shoes all ready made, upon the table. The good man knew not what to say or think at such an odd thing happening. He looked at the workmanship; there was not one false stitch in the whole job; all was so neat and true, that it was quite a masterpiece.

The same day a customer came in, and the shoes suited him so well that he willingly paid a price higher than usual for them; and the poor shoemaker, with the money, bought leather enough to make two pairs more. In the evening he cut out the work, and went to bed early, that he might get up and begin betimes next day; but he was saved all the trouble, for when he got up in the morning the work was done ready to his hand. Soon in came buyers, who paid him handsomely for his goods, so that he bought leather enough for four pair more. He cut out the work again overnight and found it done in the morning, as before; and so it went on for some time: what was got ready in the evening was always done by daybreak, and the good man soon became thriving and well off again.

One evening, about Christmas-time, as he and his wife were sitting over the fire chatting together, he said to her, ‘I should like to sit up and watch tonight, that we may see who it is that comes and does my work for me.’ The wife liked the thought; so they left a light burning, and hid themselves in a corner of the room, behind a curtain that was hung up there, and watched what would happen.

As soon as it was midnight, there came in two little naked dwarfs; and they sat themselves upon the shoemaker’s bench, took up all the work that was cut out, and began to ply with their little fingers, stitching and rapping and tapping away at such a rate, that the shoemaker was all wonder, and could not take his eyes off them. And on they went, till the job was quite done, and the shoes stood ready for use upon the table. This was long before daybreak; and then they bustled away as quick as lightning.

The next day the wife said to the shoemaker. ‘These little wights have made us rich, and we ought to be thankful to them, and do them a good turn if we can. I am quite sorry to see them run about as they do; and indeed it is not very decent, for they have nothing upon their backs to keep off the cold. I’ll tell you what, I will make each of them a shirt, and a coat and waistcoat, and a pair of pantaloons into the bargain; and do you make each of them a little pair of shoes.’

The thought pleased the good cobbler very much; and one evening, when all the things were ready, they laid them on the table, instead of the work that they used to cut out, and then went and hid themselves, to watch what the little elves would do.

About midnight in they came, dancing and skipping, hopped round the room, and then went to sit down to their work as usual; but when they saw the clothes lying for them, they laughed and chuckled, and seemed mightily delighted.

Then they dressed themselves in the twinkling of an eye, and danced and capered and sprang about, as merry as could be; till at last they danced out at the door, and away over the green.

The good couple saw them no more; but everything went well with them from that time forward, as long as they lived.
passages.attribution: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Grimms’ Fairy Tales, “The Elves and the Shoemaker,” historical English text in Project Gutenberg edition released 2001. Public domain in the USA. The source metadata does not identify this translation’s translator; no translator is asserted. Complete tale, whitespace normalized.

explanation: Cricket begins by equating best with loudest. Hearing from two places teaches him that the audience’s location matters. The scene description helps readers distinguish the nearby seats from the far bank, while the prose gives the listeners’ reactions. A lesson about attending to others fits; a claim that quiet is always best would ignore the distant listeners.

Both reading-check texts center on evidence from a listener. The main text describes a careful adjustment process, while the companion adds a second location. A report from one seat has limited reach. Connect the two sources to recommend comparing reports before another change. Loudness, speed, expression, and word accuracy are different features, not interchangeable measures of success.

Preteach Ada, Omar, cover, corner, peel, decide, and dry; compare could, would, should as a mapped family. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. passages.title: Cricket’s Two Audiences
passages.text:
Cricket practiced a bright tune beside the pond. Frog asked him to play at the evening gathering. Cricket began so loudly that the smallest listeners covered their ears. “You asked for my best tune,” he said.
Frog led him to the far bank. From there the tune sounded small. Near the stone seats it had sounded huge. Cricket tried a softer opening and asked listeners close by to signal if they could hear. Then he added a stronger middle part for those farther away. At the gathering, he watched his audience as carefully as his music. His best tune became one that others could enjoy.
Scene description: Cricket stands at center stage. Small stone seats are near the front; a second listening area is across the pond.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Checking an Aloud Reading
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: In our classroom, a reader checks that listeners can hear words clearly. A partner sits at the usual listening distance and repeats one important phrase. This gives evidence about what the listener heard.
Paragraph 2: If the phrase is unclear, the reader can adjust volume, pace, or grouping. Changing one feature at a time helps the partners notice which change helped.
Paragraph 3: The reader keeps the printed words accurate throughout. A dramatic performance that loses words does not meet the clarity goal.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.text: The class could paint the old box, or it could cover the box with paper. Ada says paint would need time to dry. Omar says paper could peel. They choose to test one small corner first. The test will help them decide what they should do.

passages.title: A Different Cricket Performance
passages.text: Original alternate version: Cricket hears one distant listener ask for more sound and plays the entire tune louder. The far listener smiles, but the nearest listeners leave their seats. Cricket has listened to one response without checking the other audience. He decides to rehearse again from both listening places before another gathering.

passages.title: Checking from Another Seat
passages.text: A second listening check uses another seat in the same classroom. The partner reports which words were clear there. One successful spot does not guarantee that every listener hears equally well. Compare the two reports before changing the reading again. The purpose is a readable performance for the actual group, not maximum loudness.

explanation: Turtle’s initial rule, shortest is best, overlooks the traveler and load. The map key makes the two routes comparable because they share endpoints but differ at the log. Re- says /ree/ and means again; play ends with ay for long a. Replay means play again. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. passages.title: The Turtle’s New Map
passages.text:
Turtle drew the shortest route from the pond to the berry clearing. It crossed a fallen log. “A straight line is best,” she told Hedgehog. Hedgehog looked at the log’s smooth, steep side. “Best for whom?” he asked.
Turtle could climb it slowly, but Hedgehog’s basket tipped when he tried. Turtle added a curved path around the log. It was longer on paper, yet Hedgehog could keep his basket level. They walked together by the curved route. At the clearing, Turtle put two lines on her map and wrote a note by each. A useful map, she decided, did more than boast about the shortest line.
Map key: straight route—crosses the log; curved route—goes around the log. Both start at POND and end at CLEARING.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Comparing Routes in a Model
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: Our classroom map shows two routes between a door and a reading corner. Route A crosses a pretend block hill. Route B goes around it. Both have the same start and destination.
Paragraph 2: Choosing a route depends on the job. A toy cart with a tall load may tip on the hill. The longer route may suit that cart because it avoids the slope.
Paragraph 3: A route label should name important features, such as steep hill or smooth floor. Distance is useful information, but it is not the only information a traveler may need.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: The Play Rehearsal
passages.text: “Can we replay that part?” asks June. Her partner nods. June reads her line slowly, then tries it with a hopeful voice. The partner listens. “I could hear the question that time,” he says. They practice once more, taking care to keep all the words.

passages.title: The Map with One Line
passages.text: Original alternate ending: Turtle erases the curved route because it looks untidy. Hedgehog follows the straight line and stops at the steep log again. When Turtle asks why he is late, he points to the spilled berries. Turtle realizes that a tidy-looking map can leave out information a traveler needs. She restores the curved route and labels the log.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Route Record
passages.text: For each model route, our record lists Start, End, and Features. The same start and end make the routes comparable. The features explain their differences. Do not enter a measured distance unless one is supplied or measured. A drawing that merely looks shorter is not an exact measurement.

Day 2: Revisit the story for synthesize a lesson, paragraph topics, and evidence with growing independence; use worksheet A as selected practice. Read A Reader’s Check independently after word preparation.

explanation: The main story connects a small visual record with a change in behavior. Wren’s remaining pebble contradicts Deer’s claim that everyone has been heard. The ending extends the lesson beyond one success: fair listening needs continued attention. The alternate uses a different tool for the same purpose. Compare the methods without declaring one universally best from a single fictional scene.

Each paragraph of the main information text has a narrow job: describe the record, distinguish hearing from agreeing, and explain review. The companion compares a spoken method with the written method. Both insist that a tool supports actual listening rather than replacing it. Use this final set to record which answers and word readings a learner manages alone and which still need adult support; the short supplied texts do not establish comprehensive grade-band complexity.

Choose the smallest useful strategy: known spelling pattern, syllable split, meaningful part, or retrieval of a taught irregular word; reread to confirm sense. Model unafraid: Read unafraid by blending un | a | fraid. Un has short u and means not; a in afraid is unstressed, like /uh/, and fraid uses ai for long a. Blend un-a-fraid to mean not afraid. Have the child point to the spellings, blend, and then reread a whole sentence to confirm meaning. Preteach strategy words sentence, blend, whole, afraid, and actor; asking for help is recorded as support, not scored as independent decoding. Before assigning passage read independently, check every word aloud with the learner; explicitly teach any additional unfamiliar correspondence or irregular word and record that help. Passage read is student practice with this preparation, not a claim that every word is newly decodable. The longer story and information passages are adult read-alouds; listening comprehension and independent word reading are recorded separately. On rereading, accuracy, phrasing, expression, and understanding matter together; guessing from pictures or racing is not the goal.

Read-aloud folktale extension: Jacobs’s traditional nest tale offers a different listening problem from Wren’s missed turn. Here pupils leave before the lesson is complete, and the remaining bird does not attend. Explain thrush, twined (wound around), lined (covered inside), and slovenly (untidy, the narrator’s judgment). The ending offers a fanciful reason for different nests; it is folklore, not a scientific account of how birds learn or build. Compare its lesson about paying attention with the original meadow tale’s lesson about giving others a chance to speak. Neither tale represents every tradition or reader.

passages.title: A Place for the Smallest Voice
passages.text:
Every animal in the meadow brought an idea for the new meeting place. Deer wanted a tall sign. Bear wanted a strong bench. Wren wanted a low branch where she could be seen while speaking. The larger animals talked over her. “We have heard everyone,” said Deer.
Mouse shook her head. She placed one pebble in a bowl for each speaker whose idea had been heard. Wren’s pebble remained beside the bowl. The animals became quiet. Wren explained her branch, and Bear found a fallen twig that would fit. Deer added a small arrow to the sign pointing toward it. At the next meeting, Mouse still brought the bowl. A good first meeting did not mean the listening job was finished.
Scene key: inside bowl—ideas heard; beside bowl—idea still waiting.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Our Discussion Record
passages.text:
Paragraph 1: A classroom discussion record can track whose idea has been heard. In this practice model, each speaker uses a chosen symbol rather than a full personal name. A mark moves from Waiting to Heard after the group listens to the idea.
Paragraph 2: The mark does not show whether the group agrees. Heard and agreed are different. A group may understand an idea and still choose another plan, with reasons.
Paragraph 3: Review the record before ending the discussion. A waiting mark invites another chance to speak. The record supports listening; it cannot replace listening to the actual words.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: A Reader’s Check
passages.text: I stop at a long word in my book. I look for a part I know. Then I blend the parts and read the sentence again. If it still sounds wrong, I ask for help with the word. I want to know what the whole sentence says.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom text.

passages.title: Listening Without the Bowl
passages.text: Original alternate version: Mouse asks each animal to name the next speaker whose idea has not been heard. They discover that Wren is still waiting. Wren explains the low branch, and the animals add it to the meeting place. This version uses a spoken turn check instead of pebbles. Both ways help the group notice a voice it missed, but either way still requires the group to listen.

passages.title: A Spoken Turn Check
passages.text: A spoken turn check asks, “Whose idea have we not heard yet?” This can reveal an overlooked speaker without moving a mark. It works only if the group pauses and attends to the answer. Like a written record, a spoken check is a tool. Its value comes from the listening action that follows it, not from saying a special question.

passages.title: The Magpie’s Nest — prose excerpt
passages.text:
All the birds of the air came to the magpie and asked her to teach them how to build nests. For the magpie is the cleverest bird of all at building nests. So she put all the birds round her and began to show them how to do it. First of all she took some mud and made a sort of round cake with it.

“Oh, that's how it's done,” said the thrush; and away it flew, and so that's how thrushes build their nests.

Then the magpie took some twigs and arranged them round in the mud.

“Now I know all about it,” says the blackbird, and off he flew; and that's how the blackbirds make their nests to this very day.

Then the magpie put another layer of mud over the twigs.

“Oh that's quite obvious,” said the wise owl, and away it flew; and owls have never made better nests since.

After this the magpie took some twigs and twined them round the outside.

“The very thing!” said the sparrow, and off he went; so sparrows make rather slovenly nests to this day.

Well, then Madge Magpie took some feathers and stuff and lined the nest very comfortably with it.

“That suits me,” cried the starling, and off it flew; and very comfortable nests have starlings.

So it went on, every bird taking away some knowledge of how to build nests, but, none of them waiting to the end. Meanwhile Madge Magpie went on working and working without, looking up till the only bird that remained was the turtle-dove, and that hadn't paid any attention all along, but only kept on saying its silly cry “Take two, Taffy, take two-o-o-o.”

At last the magpie heard this just as she was putting a twig across. So she said: “One's enough.”

But the turtle-dove kept on saying: “Take two, Taffy, take two-o-o-o.”

Then the magpie got angry and said: “One's enough I tell you.”

Still the turtle-dove cried: “Take two, Taffy, take two-o-o-o.”

At last, and at last, the magpie looked up and saw nobody near her but the silly turtle-dove, and then she got rare angry and flew away and refused to tell the birds how to build nests again. And that is why different birds build their nests differently.
passages.attribution: Joseph Jacobs, compiler, English Fairy Tales, “The Magpie’s Nest,” historical text in Project Gutenberg edition released 2005. Public domain in the USA. Complete prose narrative; the opening verse is omitted. Whitespace normalized.

items.prompt: Read these words aloud: unafraid, raincoat, silent, again. Explain the spelling pattern shared by raincoat and silent.
items.answer: Raincoat and silent each have two syllables with a long vowel in the first: rain uses ai for long a, while si is open with long i. Raincoat also has oa in coat.
steps: Inspect the actual pair: Raincoat and silent each have two syllables with a long vowel in the first: rain uses ai for long a, while si is open with long i. Raincoat also has oa in coat.

items.prompt: Compare afraid / unafraid. Explain what changes or stays the same in sound, spelling, or meaningful word parts.
items.answer: Unafraid means not afraid; the prefix changes the base meaning.

Unafraid means not afraid; the prefix changes the base meaning.

items.prompt: In The Magpie’s Nest — prose excerpt: Should this folktale be used as scientific proof of why real birds build different nests? Explain.
items.answer: No. Talking birds and the teaching episode provide a fanciful story explanation, not a scientific investigation.
steps: The ending ties nest differences to invented departures from a lesson.
A lesson about listening may be meaningful without the tale being biological evidence.
